    s_matrix[np.ix_(q, p)] = y
    s_matrix[np.ix_(p, q)] = -y.T
    h0 = h.copy()
    h0[np.ix_(p, q)] = 0
    h0[np.ix_(q, p)] = 0
    es = expm(s_matrix)
    residual = es @ h @ es.T - h0

"""Reproducible sparse-matrix-to-Zephyr experiments and reusable witnesses."""
from __future__ import annotations
import json
import pathlib
import time
import platform
import resource
import numpy as np
import networkx as nx
from compiler import compile_instance, model_graph, update_instance, complete_feasible, energy
from embedding import (make_target, CliqueTemplate, find_automatic_embedding,
    verify_embedding, allocate_physical, qubo_to_ising, graph_witness,
    physical_witness, ising_energy, versions)
from theory_checks import pause_certificate

LAB=pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
OUT=LAB/"results"


def save(name,obj):
    (OUT/name).write_text(json.dumps(obj,indent=2,allow_nan=False))


def instances(seed=20261007):
    rng=np.random.default_rng(seed)
    specs=[]
    specs.append(("banded_three_body",16,[[i,i+1,i+2] for i in range(14)]))
    specs.append(("irregular_hyperchecks",18,[sorted(rng.choice(18,size=int(rng.integers(3,6)),replace=False).tolist()) for _ in range(10)]))
    rows=[[0]+sorted(rng.choice(np.arange(1,17),size=3,replace=False).tolist()) for _ in range(10)]
    specs.append(("high_column_degree_redundant_isolate",18,rows+[rows[0],[]]))
    rows=[[] for _ in range(12)]
    for column in range(24):
        for row in rng.choice(12,size=2,replace=False): rows[int(row)].append(column)
    specs.append(("graphlike_incidence",24,rows))
    specs.append(("single_large_hypercheck",30,[list(range(30))]))
    for name,n,rows in specs:
        truth=rng.integers(0,2,size=n).tolist()
        s=[sum(truth[i] for i in row)%2 for row in rows]
        w=(rng.integers(-8,9,size=n)/4).tolist()
        yield {"name":name,"n":n,"rows":rows,"syndrome":s,"weights":w,
               "generated_feasible_pattern":truth,"seed":seed,"penalty":100.0}


def program_certificate(program,embedding,gamma=.0001,duration=100.):
    chain_set={tuple(sorted(edge)) for edges in program["chain_edges"].values() for edge in edges}
    chains=[(a,b,-program["J"][a,b]) for a,b in sorted(chain_set)]
    edges=[(a,b,j) for (a,b),j in program["J"].items() if (a,b) not in chain_set]
    return pause_certificate([embedding[i] for i in sorted(embedding)],chains,
                             program["h"],edges,gamma,duration)


def evaluate(model,target,embedding,method,rng):
    start=time.perf_counter()
    h,J,c=qubo_to_ising(model["linear"],model["quadratic"],model["offset"])
    program=allocate_physical(h,J,c,target,embedding)
    elapsed=time.perf_counter()-start
    discrepancies=[]
    for _ in range(12):
        y=rng.integers(0,2,size=len(model["linear"])).tolist()
        z={i:2*y[i]-1 for i in range(len(y))}
        physical={q:z[i] for i,branch in embedding.items() for q in branch}
        qenergy=energy(model,y)
        discrepancies.append(abs(ising_energy(program["h"],program["J"],program["offset"],physical)-program["scale"]*qenergy))
    assert max(discrepancies,default=0)<1e-8
    assert verify_embedding(model_graph(model),target,embedding)["valid"]
    assert all(-4-1e-12<=h<=4+1e-12 for h in program["h"].values())
    assert all(-1-1e-12<=j<=1+1e-12 for j in program["J"].values())
    assert all(-13-1e-12<=program["scale"]*j<=10+1e-12 for j in program["group_sums_raw"])
    cert_start=time.perf_counter();cert=program_certificate(program,embedding)
    certificate_elapsed=time.perf_counter()-cert_start
    witness=physical_witness(program)
    witness.pop("coupling_groups")
    witness["coupling_groups_reference"]="target_zephyr_g6.json"
    witness["embedding"]={str(i):list(q) for i,q in embedding.items()}
    witness["method"]=method
    witness["pause_certificate"] = cert
    summary={"method":method,**program["validation"],"scale":program["scale"],
             "scale_limiter":program["scale_limiter"],"programming_seconds":elapsed,
             "certificate_seconds":certificate_elapsed,"certificate_status":cert["status"],
             "certificate_g":cert["g"],"consistent_energy_max_error":max(discrepancies,default=0)}
    return summary,witness


def main():
    overall=time.perf_counter();rng=np.random.default_rng(714)
    target=make_target(6,t=4)
    from dwave.system.coupling_groups import coupling_groups
    targetw=graph_witness(target);targetw["coupling_groups"]=list(coupling_groups(target))
    save("target_zephyr_g6.json",targetw)
    template=CliqueTemplate(target)
    save("template_zephyr_g6.json",template.witness())
    reports=[]
    for instance in instances():
        name=instance["name"]
        save(f"input_{name}.json",instance)
        before=time.perf_counter()
        model=compile_instance(instance["rows"],instance["n"],instance["syndrome"],instance["weights"],instance["penalty"])
        compilation=time.perf_counter()-before
        graph=model_graph(model,structural=True)
        save(f"model_{name}.json",model)
        rowdegrees=[len(r) for r in model["rows"]]
        coldegrees=[sum(i in row for row in model["rows"]) for i in range(instance["n"])]
        case={"name":name,"n":instance["n"],"m":len(model["rows"]),
              "nnz":sum(rowdegrees),"max_row_degree":max(rowdegrees,default=0),
              "max_column_degree":max(coldegrees,default=0),
              "zero_columns":coldegrees.count(0),"qubo_variables":len(graph),
              "actual_edges":model_graph(model).number_of_edges(),
              "structural_edges":graph.number_of_edges(),"compilation_seconds":compilation,"mappings":[]}
        for method,prune in [("template_full",False),("template_pruned",True)]:
            before=time.perf_counter();embedding=template.embed(graph,prune=prune)
            mapping_elapsed=time.perf_counter()-before
            summary,witness=evaluate(model,target,embedding,method,rng)
            summary["embedding_seconds"]=mapping_elapsed
            case["mappings"].append(summary)
            save(f"witness_{name}_{method}.json",witness)
        # The reference sees the same stable supergraph, target, and programming constraints.
        for seed in [11,29,47]:
            reference=find_automatic_embedding(graph,target,seed=seed,timeout=5.0,tries=4)
            if reference["status"] != "valid":
                case["mappings"].append({"method":f"minorminer_{seed}",
                                         "status":reference["status"],"embedding_seconds":reference["elapsed_seconds"]})
                continue
            summary,witness=evaluate(model,target,reference["embedding"],f"minorminer_{seed}",rng)
            summary["embedding_seconds"]=reference["elapsed_seconds"]
            witness["reference_parameters"]=reference["parameters"]
            case["mappings"].append(summary)
            save(f"witness_{name}_minorminer_{seed}.json",witness)
        # New syndromes/weights: retain fixed penalty and all structural variables/edges.
        update_times=[]
        for trial in range(20):
            e=rng.integers(0,2,size=instance["n"])
            s=[int(e[row].sum()%2) for row in model["rows"]]
            weights=(rng.integers(-8,9,size=instance["n"])/4).tolist()
            before=time.perf_counter();updated=update_instance(model,s,weights)
            update_times.append(time.perf_counter()-before)
            assert updated["variables"]==model["variables"]
            assert updated["structural_edges"]==model["structural_edges"]
            assert abs(energy(updated,complete_feasible(updated,e))-float(e@np.asarray(weights)))<1e-8
        case["numeric_update_mean_seconds"]=float(np.mean(update_times))
        case["numeric_update_trials"]=len(update_times)
        reports.append(case)
        print(json.dumps({"case":name,"N":len(graph),"mapping_results":[[x["method"],x.get("physical_qubits"),x["embedding_seconds"]] for x in case["mappings"]]}),flush=True)
    # Matrix/window update: append columns/checks, rebuild logical structure,
    # and reuse only the same target's verified template.
    window=next(instances());n=window["n"]+2
    changed_rows=[list(r) for r in window["rows"]]+[[n-3,n-2,n-1]]
    e=rng.integers(0,2,size=n);s=[int(e[row].sum()%2) for row in changed_rows]
    start=time.perf_counter();changed=compile_instance(changed_rows,n,s,[.5]*n,penalty=100.)
    changed_embedding=template.embed(model_graph(changed,structural=True),prune=True)
    change_seconds=time.perf_counter()-start
    assert verify_embedding(model_graph(changed),target,changed_embedding)["valid"]
    save("matrix_update_witness.json",{"model":changed,"embedding":{str(k):v for k,v in changed_embedding.items()},"elapsed_seconds":change_seconds})
    report={"python":platform.python_version(),"versions":versions(),"seed":20261007,
            "target":{"g":6,"t":4,"nodes":len(target),"edges":target.number_of_edges(),"ideal":True},
            "template_capacity":template.capacity,"template_preprocessing_seconds":template.preprocessing_seconds,
            "conditions":{"h_range":[-4,4],"J_range":[-1,1],"coupling_group_range":[-13,10],"status":"illustrative parametric ranges, no device export","cap_scale_at_one":True},
            "matrix_update_seconds":change_seconds,"cases":reports,
            "elapsed_seconds":time.perf_counter()-overall,
            "process_maxrss_bytes_macos":resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss}
    save("experiment_summary.json",report)
    print(json.dumps({k:v for k,v in report.items() if k!="cases"},indent=2),flush=True)

if __name__=="__main__":main()

+"""Exact rational backend: all finite binary64 input weights are supported.
+
+It emits mathematical QUBO and programmed Ising coefficients as rational pairs.
+Physical ranges are parametric exact rationals. No lossy coefficient conversion
+is required by this path; a digital hardware export needs a separate precision
+certificate (provided for the ordinary regime by embedding.py).
+"""
+from __future__ import annotations
+from collections import defaultdict
+from fractions import Fraction as F
+import math
+from compiler import normalize_rows
+from embedding import verify_embedding, tree_edges, edge_key
+import networkx as nx
+
+
+def ratio(x): return [x.numerator,x.denominator]
+
+
+def compile_exact_instance(rows,n,syndrome,weights,penalty=None):
+    rows=normalize_rows(rows,n);syndrome=list(syndrome);weights=list(weights)
+    if len(rows)!=len(syndrome) or len(weights)!=n or any(s not in (0,1) for s in syndrome):
+        raise ValueError("Input dimensions/syndrome invalid")
+    if any(not math.isfinite(float(w)) for w in weights):
+        raise ValueError("Weights must be finite")
+    w=list(map(F,weights));W=sum(map(abs,w),F(0));P=W+1 if penalty is None else F(penalty)
+    if P<=W: raise ValueError("Need exact penalty greater than weight L1 norm")
+    linear=list(w);quad=defaultdict(F);constant=F(0);edges=set();constraints=[]
+    variables=[{"kind":"error","column":i} for i in range(n)]
+    def new(kind,r,stage):
+        v=len(linear);linear.append(F(0));variables.append({"kind":kind,"row":r,"stage":stage});return v
+    def square(terms,c,r):
+        nonlocal constant
+        terms=sorted(terms.items());constant+=P*c*c
+        for i,a in terms:linear[i]+=P*(a*a+2*a*c)
+        for pos,(i,a) in enumerate(terms):
+            for j,b in terms[pos+1:]:quad[i,j]+=2*P*a*b;edges.add((i,j))
+        constraints.append({"kind":"xor" if len(terms)==4 else "final","row":r,"terms":terms,"constant":c})
+    for r,(row,s) in enumerate(zip(rows,syndrome)):
+        if not row:
+            if s:raise ValueError("Nonzero empty check is infeasible")
+        elif len(row)==1:square({row[0]:1},-s,r)
+        else:
+            prev=row[0]
+            for stage,current in enumerate(row[1:]):
+                if stage==len(row)-2:
+                    sign=1-2*s;linear[prev]+=P*sign;linear[current]+=P*sign
+                    pair=edge_key(prev,current);quad[pair]-=2*P*sign;edges.add(pair);constant+=P*s
+                    constraints.append({"kind":"parity","row":r,"inputs":[prev,current],"target":s})
+                else:
+                    carry=new("carry",r,stage);parity=new("prefix",r,stage)
+                    square({prev:1,current:1,parity:-1,carry:-2},0,r);prev=parity
+    denominator=max((q.denominator for q in w),default=1)
+    step_num=math.gcd(*(abs(q.numerator)*(denominator//q.denominator) for q in w))
+    step=F(step_num,denominator) if step_num else None
+    gap=min(P-W,step) if step else P-W
+    return {"schema":"xor-chain-exact-rational-v1","n_original":n,"rows":rows,"syndrome":syndrome,
+            "weights_exact":[ratio(x) for x in w],"penalty_exact":ratio(P),"variables":variables,
+            "structural_edges":[list(e) for e in sorted(edges)],"constraints":constraints,
+            "exact_coefficients":{"linear":[ratio(a) for a in linear],
+              "quadratic":[[i,j,*ratio(a)] for (i,j),a in sorted(quad.items()) if a],"offset":ratio(constant)},
+            "numeric_certificate":{"float_ground_states_certified":False,"status":"exact_only",
+              "nonoptimal_gap_lower_bound_exact":ratio(gap),"exact_penalty_margin":ratio(P-W),
+              "weight_lattice_step_exact":None if step is None else ratio(step)}}
+
+
+def exact_graph(model,structural=True):
+    graph=nx.Graph();graph.add_nodes_from(range(len(model["variables"])))
+    graph.add_edges_from(model["structural_edges"] if structural else
+                         [(i,j) for i,j,a,b in model["exact_coefficients"]["quadratic"] if a])
+    return graph
+
+
+def exact_ising(model):
+    coeff=model["exact_coefficients"];linear=[F(*q) for q in coeff["linear"]]
+    h={i:a/2 for i,a in enumerate(linear)};J={};c=F(*coeff["offset"])+sum(linear,F(0))/2
+    for i,j,a,b in coeff["quadratic"]:
+        q=F(a,b);J[i,j]=q/4;h[i]+=q/4;h[j]+=q/4;c+=q/4
+    return h,J,c
+
+
+def allocate_symbolic(model,target,embedding,chain_margin=1,chain_factor=1,
+                      h_range=(-4,4),j_range=(-1,1),group_range=(-13,10)):
+    """Exact static embedding and signed coupling-group compliant rescaling."""
+    source=exact_graph(model,structural=False)
+    check=verify_embedding(source,target,embedding)
+    if not check["valid"]:raise ValueError("Invalid embedding")
+    margin,factor=F(chain_margin),F(chain_factor)
+    if margin<=0 or factor<1:raise ValueError("Need factor>=1,margin>0")
+    h,J,c=exact_ising(model);owners={q:i for i,b in embedding.items() for q in b};contacts={}
+    for q,r in sorted(edge_key(q,r) for q,r in target.edges):
+        if q in owners and r in owners and owners[q]!=owners[r]:
+            contacts.setdefault(edge_key(owners[q],owners[r]),(q,r))
+    ph={q:h[i]/len(branch) for i,branch in embedding.items() for q in branch}
+    pj={};load={i:abs(v) for i,v in h.items()}
+    for (i,j),v in J.items():
+        pj[edge_key(*contacts[i,j])]=v;load[i]+=abs(v);load[j]+=abs(v)
+    trees={i:tree_edges(target,b) for i,b in embedding.items()}
+    strengths={i:factor*load[i]+margin for i in embedding if trees[i]}
+    raw_offset=c
+    for i,edges in trees.items():
+        for edge in edges:pj[edge]=-strengths[i];raw_offset+=strengths[i]
+    from dwave.system.coupling_groups import coupling_groups
+    groups=list(coupling_groups(target))
+    sums=[sum((pj.get(edge_key(q,r),F(0)) for q,r in g),F(0)) for g in groups]
+    def bound(value,bounds):
+        lo,hi=map(F,bounds)
+        if not lo<0<hi:raise ValueError("Ranges must strictly contain zero")
+        return hi/value if value>0 else lo/value if value<0 else None
+    limits=[F(1)]
+    for values,bounds in [(ph.values(),h_range),(pj.values(),j_range),(sums,group_range)]:
+        for value in values:
+            lim=bound(value,bounds)
+            if lim is not None:limits.append(lim)
+    alpha=min(limits)
+    gap=F(*model["numeric_certificate"]["nonoptimal_gap_lower_bound_exact"])*alpha
+    if strengths:gap=min(gap,2*alpha*min(strengths[i]-load[i] for i in strengths))
+    return {"schema":"exact-rational-physical-v1","embedding":{str(i):list(b) for i,b in embedding.items()},
+            "h":[[q,*ratio(alpha*v)] for q,v in sorted(ph.items())],
+            "J":[[q,r,*ratio(alpha*v)] for (q,r),v in sorted(pj.items())],
+            "offset":ratio(alpha*raw_offset),"scale":ratio(alpha),
+            "nonoptimal_gap_lower_bound":ratio(gap),
+            "chain_strength_raw":{str(i):ratio(v) for i,v in strengths.items()},
+            "chain_edges":{str(i):[list(e) for e in es] for i,es in trees.items()},
+            "ranges":{"h":list(h_range),"J":list(j_range),"coupling_group":list(group_range)},
+            "group_sums":[ratio(alpha*s) for s in sums],"coupling_groups":groups,
+            "validation":check,"fidelity":"exact rational arithmetic; no coefficient rounding"}

item.stdout:
# Target construction, embedding, and programming notes

This note records the embedding subtask of this autonomous run. It used only the
run prompt, public sources, and artifacts newly written in this run. The target
is an **ideal** Zephyr graph, not an exported device working graph. The installed
generator is `dwave_networkx.zephyr_graph` 0.8.18, the predecessor of the current
`dwave.graphs.zephyr_graph` name. Every saved witness includes all target nodes,
edges, generator version, and parameters. The environment also has minorminer
0.2.21, dwave-system 1.34.0, dimod 0.12.21, networkx 3.5, and Python 3.13.2.

## Explicit polynomial construction

`CliqueTemplate(target, engine="tracks")` is the default. For integer-labeled,
ideal `Z_(g,4)` with `g>=2`, it constructs the published track embedding of
`K_(16g+1)` from Section 5.1 of [Boothby, King, and Raymond, *Zephyr Topology of
D-Wave Quantum Processors*, 2021](https://www.dwavequantum.com/media/2uznec4s/14-1056a-a_zephyr_topology_of_d-wave_quantum_processors.pdf).
A track `(u,w,k,j)` contains every `(u,w,k,j,z)` for `0<=z<g`. The branch
descriptors are implemented literally as A--E in `embedding.py`. Two branches
have length `g`; the other `16g-1` have length `2g`. Thus this complete template
uses exactly `32g^2` qubits, within the target's `32g^2+16g` qubits. This is a
known construction, not a claimed new clique-embedding result.

Here is a direct validity argument for the descriptors. External couplers join
each track. Every vertical interior track (`1<=w<=2g-1`) meets every horizontal
interior track, as follows by choosing the internal-coupler indices in the
published coordinate rule. A peripheral `w=0` track meets the opposite tracks
whose shift is zero. In descriptors B and E each branch has both orientations
of interior tracks. Descriptors C and D have one interior zero-shift track and
one perpendicular peripheral track. The two A branches are the two zero-shift
interior tracks at `w=3,k=0`. These observations give an internal connection
within each two-track branch and a contact for each pair of branches. The
descriptor ranges partition their tracks: B uses interior `w=1,2` with shift
one, C and D use the peripheral tracks and the remaining shift-zero tracks at
`w=1,2`, and E uses `w>=3`, excluding the two A tracks. Thus branch sets are
disjoint. Each constructed template is additionally checked against the exact
generated target graph before use.

For `g=1`, the code explicitly contracts a matching of the interior `K_(8,8)`:
branch `2k+j` contains `(0,1,k,j,0)` and `(1,1,k,j,0)` for `k=0,...,3`,
`j=0,1`. This gives a checked `K_8` using 16 qubits. There is no assertion that
these capacities are maximum minors. Inputs beyond capacity may still fit.

The track construction emits `O(g^2)` qubits. The ideal target has bounded
degree 20 and `O(g^2)` edges. Branch-tree construction, full clique verification,
and extraction of one contact for each logical pair each take `O(g^2)` time and
memory. The implementation traverses integer target labels and sorts only
bounded-degree neighbor lists, so it does not need a global edge sort in this
path. Serialization may separately sort witness lists. These are arithmetic
operation counts; rational bit complexity must be charged separately.

`engine="native"` retains the practical Ocean clique routine
`minorminer.busclique.find_clique_embedding(...,use_cache=False,seed=...)`.
Its default sufficient capacity is `16g-8` and observed branches are shorter.
The explicit path establishes the construction bound; the native path is an
optional measured library baseline. The [Ocean clique documentation](https://docs.dwavequantum.com/en/latest/ocean/api_ref_minorminer/source/clique_embedding.html)
describes native clique search and its caching interface. No persistent cache
was used in the measured native runs.

## Universal restriction and pruning

Once a complete template is checked, every integer-labeled graph with at most
its capacity embeds by assigning variables in sorted order to its first branch
sets. This includes isolated variables. The graph is the actual nonzero
quadratic interaction graph, not the check incidence graph.

Preprocessing fixes a spanning tree for each branch and one contact edge for
every template pair. For a new graph, mark the endpoints of the contact edges
needed by its interactions; remove nonterminal leaves from each branch tree.
An isolated variable keeps one qubit. The remaining tree is the unique minimal
subtree of the chosen tree spanning its terminals. It is nonempty and connected,
contains all required contacts, remains disjoint from other branches, and uses
no more qubits than the original branch. This proves validity and resource
nonincrease relative to this template; it does not compare quantum dynamics.

For `N` source variables, `M` interactions, and `Q<=2gN` selected full-template
qubits, a query costs `O(N log N + Q + M)` time and `O(Q+M)` working/output space.
Its logical ordering can be retained across updates. Repeated syndrome/weight
instances with unchanged graph need no new embedding query. The same reuse is
also available to any previously successful automatic embedding. If H or the
variable graph changes, a fresh query is guaranteed within capacity; a larger
graph requires another declared target/template or a search. A damaged target
must be revalidated and may invalidate the template.

`find_automatic_embedding` calls the general `minorminer.find_embedding`, then
places isolated variables and independently checks the result. Exceeding target
node/edge counts is a certified counting obstruction. An exhausted search,
insufficient leftover isolate space in a found partial embedding, or exceeding
template capacity is **not** a proof that the input has no minor embedding.

## Physical allocation and fidelity

The convention is `x_i=(1+z_i)/2`. The exact Ising conversion preserves constants.
Fields are shared uniformly over a branch; each logical coupler is placed on one
deterministically chosen available contact. Every branch has a BFS tree with
ferromagnetic coupling `-K_i`. Define

`L_i=|h_i|+sum_j |J_ij|`, and choose `K_i=chain_factor*L_i+chain_margin`

with `chain_factor>=1` and positive `chain_margin`. The physical offset is the
logical offset plus the sum of `K_i` over tree edges. Consequently the raw
physical energy of every consistent assignment equals the logical energy.

If a branch is broken, choose one monochromatic component of its tree and flip
the whole component. Every incident tree wall disappears, improving chain energy
by at least `2K_i`. The change of all nonchain terms incident to this component
is at most `2L_i`. Thus some change strictly lowers energy by at least
`2(K_i-L_i)`, and no broken state can be a global ground state. Applying this
argument until consistent proves physical ground-state fidelity. If the exact
logical nonoptimal gap is bounded below by `delta_Q`, the exact raw physical
nonoptimal gap is at least

`min(delta_Q, 2 min_(nonsingleton i)(K_i-L_i))`.

The minimum over no nonsingleton branches is omitted. The argument permits
degenerate optima and does not assume a unique correction.

All fields, logical couplers, reduction penalties, and chain couplers enter a
common positive scale `alpha`. The code supports asymmetric intervals for h and
J and signed sums of coupling strengths in the Zephyr groups generated by
`dwave.system.coupling_groups`. The [official solver-property description](https://docs.dwavequantum.com/en/latest/quantum_research/solver_properties_all.html)
states these are separate constraints. The defaults `h=(-4,4)`, `J=(-1,1)`,
and groups `(-13,10)` are illustrative parameter choices, not claimed properties
of a particular QPU. No device export was available. All alternatives in a
comparison must use the same target and these same chosen intervals. For other
Zephyr tile sizes, callers must supply the correct coupling groups explicitly.

`allocate_physical_exact` builds an exact companion from the compiler's rational
coefficients. The chosen binary64 K values and alpha are treated as exact rational
parameters, and their positive margin is checked against exact logical loads.
Let rho be the sum of absolute errors of all actual programmed h and J values
relative to that companion. If `2 rho < alpha*delta_raw`, every rounded ground
state belongs to the exact ground set. This is the elementary uniform diagonal
energy perturbation bound; it allows selection within a tied optimum. Constant
offset error is recorded but does not affect minimizers. Actual binary64 h/J and
group sums are checked using exact rational arithmetic. If necessary, alpha is
moved toward zero with `nextafter` to make every programmed constraint hold.
Failure of the sufficient fidelity certificate is explicit and means
inconclusive, not proof that the physical minimizers are wrong.

The allocator currently scans the target and groups on every program update:
`O(|E_T|+Q+M)` arithmetic work on ideal Zephyr, with rational error-certificate
work linear in programmed coefficients and group incidences. It does not claim
that these scans are already reduced to the changed weights alone. Contacts,
trees, and group membership could be cached further. This is one limitation of
the implementation's update cost.

## Checks, evidence, and limitations

`results/embed_explicit_tracks_checks.json` verifies explicit complete minors for
g=1,2,3,4,6,8,12. `embed_explicit_tracks_witness.json` contains the entire g=6
target and K97 template. Observed template preprocessing was about 20 ms at g=6
and 96 ms at g=12 in the first run; timings are observations, not asymptotic
proofs. The g=6 complete template has 1152 qubits and maximum branch length 12.

`results/embed_checks.json` records all 1024 graphs on five vertices surviving
template pruning, six kinds of invalid embeddings rejected, 496 QUBO-to-Ising
assignment checks, and physical consistency/ground-state checks on small models.
`embed_physical_witness.json` is an independently inspectable small programmed
model. Additional exact numeric-certificate checks are recorded in the same file.

The separate `embed_benchmark.json` and `embed_target_and_witnesses.json` preserve
the initial nine-graph **native-template** experiment on the same ideal g=4
target, with three seeded automatic reference runs per graph. Graphs include
paths, random cubic graphs, and seeded Erdos-Renyi graphs of 24,40,56 variables.
Native full-template counts were 120,200,280 respectively. Pruned counts ranged
37--246; automatic outputs ranged 24--244. Automatic embedding usually used
fewer physical qubits, while pruned-template queries were faster. Template
queries exclude independent revalidation, whereas the recorded automatic call
includes it; both timing components are given. No claim of overall quality or
annealing superiority follows from these observations. Parent-run matrix
experiments provide the decoding-specific comparison.

Two initial invocations of the uncached native clique routine at g=1 stalled
and later exited with code 137; the precise cause was not diagnosed. This
affected exploratory checks, not saved successful timings. The explicit g=1
construction above avoids that call. The g>=2 native runs completed normally.

Reproduce these checks without credentials:

```sh
python /absolute/path/to/lab/scripts/embedding_checks.py --output /absolute/path/to/lab/results
```

The guarantees concern valid minors, faithful final classical ground states,
explicit programming constraints, finite-precision certification, and
resource/processing costs. Any annealing-path theorem is separate; a smaller
branch count, shorter chain, or larger final-energy scale alone does not prove
better finite-time quantum-annealing success.

# Target construction, embedding, and programming notes

run prompt, public sources, and artifacts newly written in this run. The target
is an **ideal** Zephyr graph, not an exported device working graph. The installed
generator is `dwave_networkx.zephyr_graph` 0.8.18, the predecessor of the current
`dwave.graphs.zephyr_graph` name. Every saved witness includes all target nodes,
edges, generator version, and parameters. The environment also has minorminer
0.2.21, dwave-system 1.34.0, dimod 0.12.21, networkx 3.5, and Python 3.13.2.

## Explicit polynomial construction

`CliqueTemplate(target, engine="tracks")` is the default. For integer-labeled,
ideal `Z_(g,4)` with `g>=2`, it constructs the published track embedding of
`K_(16g+1)` from Section 5.1 of [Boothby, King, and Raymond, *Zephyr Topology of
D-Wave Quantum Processors*, 2021](https://www.dwavequantum.com/media/2uznec4s/14-1056a-a_zephyr_topology_of_d-wave_quantum_processors.pdf).
A track `(u,w,k,j)` contains every `(u,w,k,j,z)` for `0<=z<g`. The branch
descriptors are implemented literally as A--E in `embedding.py`. Two branches
have length `g`; the other `16g-1` have length `2g`. Thus this complete template
uses exactly `32g^2` qubits, within the target's `32g^2+16g` qubits. This is a
known construction, not a claimed new clique-embedding result.

Here is a direct validity argument for the descriptors. External couplers join
each track. Every vertical interior track (`1<=w<=2g-1`) meets every horizontal
interior track, as follows by choosing the internal-coupler indices in the
published coordinate rule. A peripheral `w=0` track meets the opposite tracks
whose shift is zero. In descriptors B and E each branch has both orientations
of interior tracks. Descriptors C and D have one interior zero-shift track and
one perpendicular peripheral track. The two A branches are the two zero-shift
interior tracks at `w=3,k=0`. These observations give an internal connection
within each two-track branch and a contact for each pair of branches. The
descriptor ranges partition their tracks: B uses interior `w=1,2` with shift
one, C and D use the peripheral tracks and the remaining shift-zero tracks at
`w=1,2`, and E uses `w>=3`, excluding the two A tracks. Thus branch sets are
disjoint. Each constructed template is additionally checked against the exact
generated target graph before use.

For `g=1`, the code explicitly contracts a matching of the interior `K_(8,8)`:
branch `2k+j` contains `(0,1,k,j,0)` and `(1,1,k,j,0)` for `k=0,...,3`,
`j=0,1`. This gives a checked `K_8` using 16 qubits. There is no assertion that
these capacities are maximum minors. Inputs beyond capacity may still fit.

The track construction emits `O(g^2)` qubits. The ideal target has bounded
degree 20 and `O(g^2)` edges. Branch-tree construction, full clique verification,
and extraction of one contact for each logical pair each take `O(g^2)` time and
memory. The implementation traverses integer target labels and sorts only
bounded-degree neighbor lists, so it does not need a global edge sort in this
path. Serialization may separately sort witness lists. These are arithmetic
operation counts; rational bit complexity must be charged separately.

`engine="native"` retains the practical Ocean clique routine
`minorminer.busclique.find_clique_embedding(...,use_cache=False,seed=...)`.
Its default sufficient capacity is `16g-8` and observed branches are shorter.
The explicit path establishes the construction bound; the native path is an
optional measured library baseline. The [Ocean clique documentation](https://docs.dwavequantum.com/en/latest/ocean/api_ref_minorminer/source/clique_embedding.html)
describes native clique search and its caching interface. No persistent cache
was used in the measured native runs.

## Universal restriction and pruning

Once a complete template is checked, every integer-labeled graph with at most
its capacity embeds by assigning variables in sorted order to its first branch
sets. This includes isolated variables. The graph is the actual nonzero
quadratic interaction graph, not the check incidence graph.

Preprocessing fixes a spanning tree for each branch and one contact edge for
every template pair. For a new graph, mark the endpoints of the contact edges
needed by its interactions; remove nonterminal leaves from each branch tree.
An isolated variable keeps one qubit. The remaining tree is the unique minimal
subtree of the chosen tree spanning its terminals. It is nonempty and connected,
contains all required contacts, remains disjoint from other branches, and uses
no more qubits than the original branch. This proves validity and resource
nonincrease relative to this template; it does not compare quantum dynamics.

For `N` source variables, `M` interactions, and `Q<=2gN` selected full-template
qubits, a query costs `O(N log N + Q + M)` time and `O(Q+M)` working/output space.
Its logical ordering can be retained across updates. Repeated syndrome/weight
instances with unchanged graph need no new embedding query. The same reuse is
also available to any previously successful automatic embedding. If H or the
variable graph changes, a fresh query is guaranteed within capacity; a larger
graph requires another declared target/template or a search. A damaged target
must be revalidated and may invalidate the template.

`find_automatic_embedding` calls the general `minorminer.find_embedding`, then
places isolated variables and independently checks the result. Exceeding target
node/edge counts is a certified counting obstruction. An exhausted search,
insufficient leftover isolate space in a found partial embedding, or exceeding
template capacity is **not** a proof that the input has no minor embedding.

The convention is `x_i=(1+z_i)/2`. The exact Ising conversion preserves constants.

deterministically chosen available contact. Every branch has a BFS tree with

Fields are shared uniformly over a branch; each logical coupler is placed on one
deterministically chosen available contact. Every branch has a BFS tree with
ferromagnetic coupling `-K_i`. Define

`L_i=|h_i|+sum_j |J_ij|`, and choose `K_i=chain_factor*L_i+chain_margin`

with `chain_factor>=1` and positive `chain_margin`. The physical offset is the
logical offset plus the sum of `K_i` over tree edges. Consequently the raw
physical energy of every consistent assignment equals the logical energy.

If a branch is broken, choose one monochromatic component of its tree and flip
the whole component. Every incident tree wall disappears, improving chain energy
by at least `2K_i`. The change of all nonchain terms incident to this component
is at most `2L_i`. Thus some change strictly lowers energy by at least
`2(K_i-L_i)`, and no broken state can be a global ground state. Applying this
argument until consistent proves physical ground-state fidelity. If the exact
logical nonoptimal gap is bounded below by `delta_Q`, the exact raw physical
nonoptimal gap is at least

`min(delta_Q, 2 min_(nonsingleton i)(K_i-L_i))`.

The minimum over no nonsingleton branches is omitted. The argument permits
degenerate optima and does not assume a unique correction.

All fields, logical couplers, reduction penalties, and chain couplers enter a
common positive scale `alpha`. The code supports asymmetric intervals for h and
J and signed sums of coupling strengths in the Zephyr groups generated by
`dwave.system.coupling_groups`. The [official solver-property description](https://docs.dwavequantum.com/en/latest/quantum_research/solver_properties_all.html)
states these are separate constraints. The defaults `h=(-4,4)`, `J=(-1,1)`,
and groups `(-13,10)` are illustrative parameter choices, not claimed properties
of a particular QPU. No device export was available. All alternatives in a
comparison must use the same target and these same chosen intervals. For other
Zephyr tile sizes, callers must supply the correct coupling groups explicitly.

`allocate_physical_exact` builds an exact companion from the compiler's rational
coefficients. The chosen binary64 K values and alpha are treated as exact rational
parameters, and their positive margin is checked against exact logical loads.
Let rho be the sum of absolute errors of all actual programmed h and J values
relative to that companion. If `2 rho < alpha*delta_raw`, every rounded ground
state belongs to the exact ground set. This is the elementary uniform diagonal
energy perturbation bound; it allows selection within a tied optimum. Constant
offset error is recorded but does not affect minimizers. Actual binary64 h/J and
group sums are checked using exact rational arithmetic. If necessary, alpha is
moved toward zero with `nextafter` to make every programmed constraint hold.
Failure of the sufficient fidelity certificate is explicit and means
inconclusive, not proof that the physical minimizers are wrong.

The allocator currently scans the target and groups on every program update:
`O(|E_T|+Q+M)` arithmetic work on ideal Zephyr, with rational error-certificate
work linear in programmed coefficients and group incidences. It does not claim
that these scans are already reduced to the changed weights alone. Contacts,
trees, and group membership could be cached further. This is one limitation of
the implementation's update cost.

## Checks, evidence, and limitations

`results/embed_explicit_tracks_checks.json` verifies explicit complete minors for
g=1,2,3,4,6,8,12. `embed_explicit_tracks_witness.json` contains the entire g=6
target and K97 template. Observed template preprocessing was about 20 ms at g=6
and 96 ms at g=12 in the first run; timings are observations, not asymptotic
proofs. The g=6 complete template has 1152 qubits and maximum branch length 12.

`results/embed_checks.json` records all 1024 graphs on five vertices surviving
template pruning, six kinds of invalid embeddings rejected, 496 QUBO-to-Ising
assignment checks, and physical consistency/ground-state checks on small models.
`embed_physical_witness.json` is an independently inspectable small programmed
model. Additional exact numeric-certificate checks are recorded in the same file.

The separate `embed_benchmark.json` and `embed_target_and_witnesses.json` preserve
the initial nine-graph **native-template** experiment on the same ideal g=4
target, with three seeded automatic reference runs per graph. Graphs include
paths, random cubic graphs, and seeded Erdos-Renyi graphs of 24,40,56 variables.
Native full-template counts were 120,200,280 respectively. Pruned counts ranged
37--246; automatic outputs ranged 24--244. Automatic embedding usually used
fewer physical qubits, while pruned-template queries were faster. Template
queries exclude independent revalidation, whereas the recorded automatic call
includes it; both timing components are given. No claim of overall quality or
annealing superiority follows from these observations. Parent-run matrix
experiments provide the decoding-specific comparison.

Two initial invocations of the uncached native clique routine at g=1 stalled
and later exited with code 137; the precise cause was not diagnosed. This
affected exploratory checks, not saved successful timings. The explicit g=1
construction above avoids that call. The g>=2 native runs completed normally.

Reproduce these checks without credentials:

```sh
python /absolute/path/to/lab/scripts/embedding_checks.py --output /absolute/path/to/lab/results
```

The guarantees concern valid minors, faithful final classical ground states,
explicit programming constraints, finite-precision certification, and
resource/processing costs. Any annealing-path theorem is separate; a smaller
branch count, shorter chain, or larger final-energy scale alone does not prove
better finite-time quantum-annealing success.
"}

L52@P3: 1 Introduction
L53@P3: This paper describes D-Wave’s upcoming annealing processor topology; that is, the pattern
L54@P3: that defines how the processor’s qubits and couplers interconnect.
L55@P3: Zephyr is a significant advancement over D-Wave’s previous Pegasus and Chimera topologies, available in the Advantage and D-Wave 2000Q products respectively. Zephyr features
L56@P3: qubits of degree 20 and native K4 and K8,8 subgraphs.
L57@P3: 2 The Zephyr Topology
L58@P3: In Zephyr, as in Pegasus and Chimera, qubits are oriented vertically or horizontally. Chimera
L59@P3: has two types of coupler: internal couplers connect pairs of orthogonal (with opposite orientation) qubits, and external couplers connect colinear pairs of qubits (that is, pairs of
L60@P3: qubits that are parallel, in the same row or column). The Pegasus family has, in addition to
L61@P3: Chimera’s internal and external couplers, a third type: odd couplers. Odd couplers connect
L62@P3: parallel qubit pairs in adjacent rows or columns. The Zephyr topology features these three
L63@P3: coupler types, with a total of two odd couplers, two external couplers, and sixteen internal
L64@P3: couplers.
L65@P3: In the Chimera topology, qubits have a nominal length of 4 (each qubit is connected to 4
L66@P3: orthogonal qubits through internal couplers) and degree of 6 (each qubit is connected to 6
L67@P3: different qubits through couplers). In the Pegasus family, qubits have a nominal length of
L68@P3: 12 and degree of 15. In the Zephyr topology, qubits have a nominal length of 16 and degree
L69@P3: of 20.
L70@P3: 2.1 Formulaic Description
L71@P3: In broad strokes, a Zephyr graph with grid parameter m and tile parameter t, notated Zm,t
L72@P3: (or simply Zm when t = 4), contains 8tm2+4tm qubits, and has maximum degree 4t+4. For
L73@P3: example, a Z15 graph contains 7440 qubits in total. Abstractly speaking, a Zephyr graph can
L74@P3: be constructed by first constructing a Chimera graph C2m+1,2m+1,t, adding odd couplers,
L75@P3: joining qubits into pairs along tile boundaries in an alternating fashion, and finally deleting
L76@P3: unpaired qubits on the periphery. This construction is shown in 1, but not elaborated in full
L77@P3: rigor.
L78@P3: We enumerate the qubits of Zm with vectors of length 5, where a qubit (u, w, k, j, z) has
L79@P3: coordinates
L80@P3: • u is the orientation, indicating if a qubit is vertical (u = 0) or horizontal (u = 1).
L81@P3: • w is the perpendicular block offset, indicating the index of the qubit’s tile, in the
L82@P3: orientation perpendicular to u, with 0 ≤ w < 2m + 1. (That is, if u = 0, then w is a
L83@P3: horizontal (column) index, and if u = 1, then w is a vertical (row) index.)
L84@P3: • k is the qubit index, indicating the index of a qubit within a tile, and 0 ≤ k < t.
L85@P3-4: Copyright © D-Wave Systems Inc.Zephyr Topology 2
L86@P4: Figure 1: Construction of the Zephyr lattice Z1 from a Chimera C3,3,8. (top left) The C3,3,8
L87@P4: graph in the point-and-line drawing style, with black nodes, edges to be contracted in orange, and
L88@P4: remaining edges grey. (top right) The same C3,3,8 graph drawn in qubit-loop style, with internal
L89@P4: edges drawn as grey circles, and odd and external couplers drawn as barbells colored as above.
L90@P4: (bottom left) The Z1 graph drawn in point-and-line style. (bottom right) The Z1 graph drawn
L91@P4: in qubit-loop style.
L92@P4-5: Copyright © D-Wave Systems Inc.Zephyr Topology 3
L93@P5: • j is the shift identifier, with j = 0 to indicate that a qubit is shifted to the left/top
L94@P5: and j = 1 to indicate that a qubit is shifted to the right/bottom.
L95@P5: • z is the parallel tile offset, indicating the index of the qubit’s tile in the orientation
L96@P5: parallel to u, with 0 ≤ z < m. (That is, if u = 0, then z is a vertical (row) index, and
L97@P5: if u = 1, then z is a horizontal (column) index.)
L98@P5: In the following description of the three types of couplers, a coupler p ∼ q exists whenever
L99@P5: both p and q are qubits in Zm,t. The three sets of Zephyr couplers are:
L100@P5: • external: (u, w, k, j, z) ∼ (u, w, k, j, z + 1)
L101@P5: • odd: (u, w, k, 0, z) ∼ (u, w, k, 1, z − α) for α ∈ {0, 1}
L102@P5: • internal: (0, 2w + 1 − α, k, j, z − jβ) ∼ (1, 2z + 1 − β, h, i, w − iα) for α ∈ {0, 1} and
L103@P5: β ∈ {0, 1}

L105@P5: (u, w, k, j, z) 7→ z + m(j + 2(k + t(w + (2m + 1)u))),
L106@P5: which is a bijection between the 8tm2 + 4tm coordinate labels and the interval
L107@P5: {0, · · · , 8tm2 + 4tm}.
L108@P5: 2.2 Clique and Bipartite Embeddings for Problem Solving
L109@P5: As we did with the Pegasus family, we use the fact that Zephyr (with odd couplers removed)
L110@P5: can be viewed as a graph minor of Chimera to ease the computation of efficient clique
L111@P5: embeddings. Optimal embeddings of complete graphs, ε : Ka → Z consist of a parallel
L112@P5: paths of horizontal qubits and a parallel paths of vertical qubits, connected at a point of
L113@P5: intersection to make a chains. The algorithm of [1] can be modified to produce embeddings
L114@P5: with chains of length m. For graphs with full yield, the resulting embedding is equivalent
L115@P5: (albeit with shorter chains) to an embedding in a full-yield Chimera C2m−1,2m−1,2t (the
L116@P5: square Chimera graph obtained by deleting the peripheral cells of C2m+1,2m+1,2t). Thus,
L117@P5: the size of this embedding is 2(2m − 1)t, or 16m − 8 when t is 4.
L118@P5: Likewise, the largest useful complete bipartite graphs are obtained by working within the
L119@P5: non-peripheral square. Complete bipartite embeddings ε : Ka,b → Z consist of a parallel
L120@P5: paths of horizontal qubits, each in a different row, and b parallel paths of vertical qubits,
L121@P5: each in a different column. This gives an embedding of K2(2m−1)t,2(2m−1)t (or K16m−8,16m−8
L122@P5: when t is 4), where all chains have length m.
L123@P5: 3 Lattice Embeddings
L124@P5: Recent work has shown great promise in the simulation of two- and three-dimensional quantum magnetic systems using quantum annealers [2, 3]. In Pegasus, embedding of 3D lattices

L131@P7: chains. However, several examples show that embedding low-dimensional lattices in Zephyr
L132@P7: is easier than in Pegasus. Fig. 2 shows a Z3,1 graph, wherein a direct embedding of a
L133@P7: checkerboard lattice is clearly visible. In Chimera and Pegasus, qubit spin ice [5] has been
L134@P7: implemented using four-qubit chains and two-qubit chains, respectively. In Zephyr, this can
L135@P7: be done with one-qubit chains, with no translation between the logical and embedded systems. As an immediate consequence of the direct embedding of a checkerboard lattice, we

L137@P7: embedding in Chimera took four-qubit chains [8]. Thus we can expect the Zephyr topology
L138@P7: to provide a rich testbed for effectively probing quantum effects in materials.

text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: /Users/home/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/Research/[Mercor]SciCode2/benchmarks/qec-annealing-embedding/labs/lab-002-agent-test-general-h/RESEARCH_REPORT.md
+# General sparse decoding compilation with a conditional annealing certificate
+
+## Result and completion scope
+
+This trial developed an executable, general sparse-matrix compiler, an explicit
+polynomial construction of a valid ideal-Zephyr embedding in a declared size
+regime, exact and certified floating coefficient allocation, and an efficient
+finite-time quantum-dynamics certificate. The certificate gives an actual
+ordering for one decoding pause protocol and proves that the ordering reverses
+when the initial correction changes. These results meet the three stated
+acceptance criteria within the explicitly allowed conditional theoretical
+regime. They do **not** establish a universal ranking, complete forward-anneal
+speedup, or performance on a noisy QPU.
+
+The chosen contribution is the connection between a reusable general interface,
+a deterministic construction with checkable witnesses, and an inexpensive
+certificate of when an embedding prevents useful logical transitions. Local XOR
+reductions and the published Zephyr clique construction are established tools;
+no priority claim is made for those components. The finite-time proof and its
+explicit constants are derived in full in [THEORY_CERTIFICATE.md](THEORY_CERTIFICATE.md).
+
+The default explicit template was faster to query than the automatic reference
+on all five matrix examples, but used more physical qubits. The usual chain
+strengths gave **inconclusive** dynamical certificates for all 25 broad-example
+mappings. The positive dynamical comparison is deliberately restricted to its
+proved regime; these inconclusive outcomes are retained as part of the result.
+
+## Assignment, resources, and scientific process
+
+- Original shared trial start: **2026-10-07 19:55:30.405 UTC**, or 12:55:30.405 PDT.
+- Total authorized budget: **7,200 elapsed seconds**; deadline
+  **2026-10-07 21:55:30.405 UTC**. Preflight and reading count toward this budget.
+- This scientific solver launched at **20:11:04.521 UTC**, leaving
+  **104 minutes 25.884 seconds**. It did not restart or extend the deadline.
+- Final measured finish and elapsed times are recorded in
+  [results/scientific_completion.json](results/scientific_completion.json).
+- Solver session: `01a117fd-a459-7621-b36c-1c49df7bcbbf`.
+- The two scientific assistants worked on independent scopes: the pause proof
+  and its validation (`01a117fe-0bfd-7be3-bceb-77efccafaa8b`), and the embedding,
+  programming, and automatic-reference implementation
+  (`01a117fe-343f-7a11-96fa-c440be5b285c`). The coordinator verified all three
+  scientific sessions as Astra/ultra and owns the separate run/transcript records.
+
+Only the frozen prompt, public references/software, and this run's newly created
+materials were used scientifically. No sibling lab, author solution, or previous
+trial was consulted. The coordinator prepared procedural provenance and later
+ran read-only checks; it supplied no scientific hints during this solve.
+
+Python 3.13.2 and the pinned packages in [requirements.txt](requirements.txt)
+were already installed. No QPU credentials or QPU were used. The final experiment
+summary records measured wall times and macOS process maximum RSS. These are
+local observations, not calibrated cross-machine benchmarks. No unmeasured QPU
+time, energy usage, or logical error rate is inferred.
+
+## 1. Matrix-to-QUBO construction and proof
+
+The input is a row-support representation of any binary matrix, the column
+count `n`, a promised valid syndrome, and finite additive weights. Duplicate
+sparse coordinates cancel over GF(2). Dependent and empty rows, isolated
+columns, negative/zero weights, and columns incident on arbitrarily many checks
+are supported. No graphlike or code-family assumption is made. The compiler
+does not solve the decoding optimization as preprocessing.
+
+Write `k=nnz(H)`, row degrees `d_r`, and choose
+
+\[
+ W=\sum_i|w_i|,\qquad \Lambda>W.
+\]
+
+For a row of degree at least three, sequentially compute prefix parity using
+binary parity and carry variables, with local factors
+
+\[
+ \Lambda(a+b-p-2t)^2.
+\]
+
+This factor is zero exactly when `p=a XOR b` and `t=floor((a+b)/2)`;
+otherwise it is at least `Lambda`. Terminate each row with the exact quadratic
+two-input parity-violation indicator
+
+\[
+ \Lambda\{s+(1-2s)(a+b-2ab)\}.
+\]
+
+A degree-one row uses `Lambda(e_i-s)^2`. An empty row requires syndrome zero.
+The full QUBO is the additive cost plus all these nonnegative integer-valued
+penalties. Its projection is simply the first `n` error variables. For
+
+\[
+ a=2\sum_r(d_r-2)_+,\quad L=n+a,
+\]
+
+there are exactly `a` auxiliary variables and at most
+
+\[
+ E\leq\sum_{r:d_r\ge2}\{6(d_r-2)+1\}
+\]
+
+structural quadratic edges. Aggregation may remove interactions through exact
+cancellation. The compiler records both this stable structural envelope and the
+actual nonzero graph; embeddings of the envelope are also valid for the actual
+graph. Syndrome changes can change interaction signs and cancellation, so reuse
+is based on the envelope, not an unjustified fixed actual graph assumption.
+
+**Fidelity.** Every feasible error pattern has a unique zero-penalty extension,
+with QUBO energy equal to its cost. If any factor is violated, QUBO energy is at
+least `C_min + Lambda`, where `C_min=sum_i min(0,w_i)`. Every feasible cost is at
+most `C_max=sum_i max(0,w_i)`, and `C_max-C_min=W`. Thus every violating state
+has energy greater than every feasible optimum. Exactly all minimum-cost
+feasible error patterns occur as projected exact QUBO ground states. Negative
+weights and ties do not change this argument. No hidden true error or observable
+outcome is supplied to the decoder; the generated feasible patterns only
+construct valid test syndromes. We do not report logical failure because no
+observable map was evaluated.
+
+The main implementation is [scripts/compiler.py](scripts/compiler.py). The
+exact-only implementation [scripts/exact_pipeline.py](scripts/exact_pipeline.py)
+uses rational arithmetic throughout and also handles cases where an otherwise
+valid penalty or intermediate coefficient exceeds binary64 range. It accepts
+all finite binary64 weights, including subnormal and very large values. The
+mathematical construction holds for finite real weights under exact arithmetic;
+the executable exact backend represents rational inputs.
+
+**Numerical fidelity is checked, not assumed.** Binary64 input weights have
+exact rational values. Let `delta_w` be the positive gcd lattice spacing of
+those rational weights, or infinity if all weights vanish. Then
+
+\[
+ \delta_Q=\min(\Lambda-W,\delta_w)>0
+\]
+
+lower-bounds the energy difference between an exact ground state and every
+nonoptimal QUBO assignment. If the sum of absolute nonconstant coefficient
+rounding errors is `rho`, the sufficient condition `2 rho < delta_Q` ensures
+every rounded QUBO ground state is an exact optimum. Exactly tied optima may be
+split, which is allowed by the prompt. Exact coefficients and this certificate
+are saved. The binary64 compiler rejects uncertified expansions; the exact
+backend preserves the mathematical model. For example, naively adding a
+weight `1e-300` to a penalty of one can erase the strict optimum. Our tests
+confirm this unsafe floating expansion is rejected and its exact counterpart
+remains faithful.
+
+## 2. Embedding and programming
+
+The target is ideal `Z_(g,4)`, generated by installed
+`dwave_networkx.zephyr_graph` 0.8.18. The current `dwave.graphs` module was absent;
+the legacy generator's exact nodes/edges, version, and parameters are saved in
+[results/target_zephyr_g6.json](results/target_zephyr_g6.json). This is explicitly
+an ideal architecture, not an actual working graph. No nonhardware edge is used.
+
+For `g>=2`, the default constructs the published track minor of `K_(16g+1)`;
+the complete template has `32g^2` qubits and maximum branch size `2g`.
+The `g=1` special case explicitly contracts an interior `K_(8,8)` matching to
+obtain `K_8`. These are sufficient capacities, not maximal-minor claims.
+Construction and verification are `O(g^2)` on the bounded-degree ideal graph.
+The exact coordinate construction and its validity proof are in
+[TARGET_NOTES.md](TARGET_NOTES.md), based on Section 5.1 of the public
+[Zephyr topology report](https://www.dwavequantum.com/media/2uznec4s/14-1056a-a_zephyr_topology_of_d-wave_quantum_processors.pdf).
+
+Preprocessing stores a connected tree for every template branch and one target
+contact edge for every pair. Any model with `L<=16g+1` is embedded by selecting
+its branches. For each needed structural edge, mark its two contact endpoints;
+prune unmarked leaves from each selected branch tree. Isolated variables retain
+one physical qubit. The remaining branch is connected, nonempty, disjoint, and
+contains every necessary contact. It cannot use more qubits than its unpruned
+template branch. This is a deterministic guarantee of validity and resource
+nonincrease relative to the fixed template, not a dynamics comparison.
+
+The CLI can instead use a supplied target graph and the automatic minorminer
+reference. An explicit-template capacity failure or failed heuristic search is
+reported as unresolved, not as impossibility. Actual logical vertex or edge
+counts exceeding corresponding target counts are certified necessary
+obstructions. A damaged target must be revalidated; no ideal-template guarantee
+is silently transferred to it.
+
+For `e_i=(1+z_i)/2`, a QUBO with linear coefficients `a_i`, quadratic
+coefficients `b_ij`, and constant `c_Q` becomes
+
+\[
+ J_{ij}=b_{ij}/4,\quad h_i=a_i/2+\sum_j b_{ij}/4,
+ \quad c=c_Q+\sum_i a_i/2+\sum_{ij}b_{ij}/4.
+\]
+
+Allocate a field uniformly over each branch, put each logical coupling on one
+available contact, and use ferromagnetic tree couplings `-K_i`. With
+
+\[
+ L_i=|h_i|+\sum_j|J_{ij}|,\qquad K_i=fL_i+\mu,
+ \quad f\ge1,\ \mu>0,
+\]
+
+the physical offset `c + sum_(chain edges) K_i` makes every consistent raw
+physical energy exactly equal to its logical QUBO energy. In a broken branch,
+flipping a monochromatic tree component eliminates at least one wall, saving
+at least `2K_i`, and changes nonchain energy by at most `2L_i`. Thus every
+broken state admits a strict improvement. All physical ground states are
+consistent and project onto minimum-cost corrections. A sufficient physical
+nonoptimal gap before rescaling is
+
+\[
+ \delta_{\rm phys,raw}=\min\left(\delta_Q,
+       2\min_{i:\,|C_i|>1}(K_i-L_i)\right),
+\]
+
+omitting the second minimum when all branches are singletons.
+
+One positive scale `alpha` applies to every field, reduction coefficient, chain
+coupling, and offset. It is the minimum of the applicable positive bounds from
+individual h/J intervals and signed coupling-group sums. Our common illustrative
+constraints are `h in [-4,4]`, `J in [-1,1]`, and group sums in `[-13,10]`;
+these are parameters, not a device export. The Zephyr groups are produced by
+`dwave.system.coupling_groups` and saved. Their relevance and signed-sum meaning
+follow the [official solver-properties documentation](https://docs.dwavequantum.com/en/latest/quantum_research/solver_properties_all.html).
+
+The exact-only allocator emits rational programmed coefficients and scales.
+The practical allocator constructs an exact rational companion, compares every
+actual binary64 coefficient against it, checks all ranges and group sums using
+exact arithmetic, and certifies `2 rho_phys < alpha delta_phys,raw`. A downward
+`nextafter` scale adjustment fixes representational boundary overshoot when
+needed. Uncertified cases remain exact-only rather than receiving a false
+floating-ground-state claim. Actual device precision/noise would require an
+additional perturbation bound and is not assumed here.
+
+## 3. Efficient annealing evaluation and a proved comparison
+
+The physical model is the prompt's transverse-field Hamiltonian at a fixed
+anneal coordinate, held constant for time `t`, with no bath or control noise and
+`hbar=1`. All coefficients already include hardware scaling. Write
+
+\[
+ H=C+D-\Gamma\sum_qX_q,\quad
+ C=\sum_{qr\in E_c}c_{qr}(1-Z_qZ_r),\quad
+ \Gamma=A/2,\ c_{qr}=B|J^{\rm chain}_{qr}|/2.
+\]
+
+`D` contains the scaled diagonal problem terms, including reduction penalties.
+Let `P` be the entire consistent-branch subspace, including every logical
+assignment, not only ground states. Let `R` bound `||D||` by the sum of absolute
+coefficients, `Delta` be twice the smallest weighted chain cut, `N_p` the
+physical-qubit count, `n_1,n_2` the numbers of branches of sizes one and two,
+and `M_p=N_p-n_1`. Define
+
+\[
+ g=\Delta-2R-\Gamma(N_p+n_1),\qquad
+ b=\Gamma\sqrt{M_p+2n_2}.
+\]
+
+If `g>0`, the proved uniform finite-time bound is
+
+\[
+ \left\|(e^{-itH}-e^{-itPHP})P\right\|
+ \leq \varepsilon(t)
+ =\frac{2b}{g}+t\frac{b^2}{g}e^{2b/g}.
+\]
+
+The exact off-block norm is `b`, because two single-qubit flips return a chain
+to its code space only by undoing one flip or flipping both sites of a size-two
+branch. A Sylvester equation separates the two ordered spectral blocks; an
+explicit anti-Hermitian conjugation cancels the first-order block coupling.
+The bounded remainder and Duhamel's formula give the displayed constants. The
+complete derivation is in the companion proof note and handles all degeneracy.
+
+Within `P`, the first-order Hamiltonian is precisely
+`D_logical - Gamma sum_(singleton i) X_i`. Diagonal events depending only on
+nonsingleton logical variables therefore remain constant under that projected
+evolution. Starting inside `P` with zero probability of such an event, its actual
+probability after the hold is at most `min(1,epsilon^2)`. The event may include
+all tied decoding optima and may extend to broken states through any fixed
+recovery rule that agrees on consistent branches. This is a certificate of
+logical-transition suppression, useful either to reject a repair mapping or to
+certify retention. An initial leakage extension is stated in the proof note.
+
+For tree branches, evaluation is linear in the programmed model size and uses
+no spectral simulation. The implementation computes its algebraic gap with
+exact rational arithmetic, bounds the square root and exponential upward, and
+rounds reported upper bounds outward. For cyclic branches it uses a conservative
+minimum-edge cut lower bound. If its conditions fail it returns **inconclusive**;
+if the bound exceeds one it marks the probability guarantee as vacuous. Dense
+matrix computations are used only in small validation examples.
+
+**A strict decoding comparison.** Use `H=[1 1]`, `s=1`, and `w=(0,0)`.
+The compiler can use `Lambda=0.0002`, producing Ising `J=0.0001` with both `01`
+and `10` optimal. The common ideal Zephyr target contains path `[0,1,2,3]`.
+The native mapping uses singletons `{1},{2}`; the encoded mapping uses
+`{0,1},{2,3}` with chain strength one. Both use the same problem coefficient,
+target, field/coupling/group constraints, `A=0.04`, `B=2`, and a constant hold
+
+\[
+ t=\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{J^2+4\Gamma^2}}\simeq39.26978545,
+ \qquad \Gamma=0.02.
+\]
+
+Starting in encoded error pattern `00`, the native exact success probability is
+
+\[
+ p_{\rm native}(t)=\frac{2\Gamma^2}{J^2+4\Gamma^2}
+       \sin^2(t\sqrt{J^2+4\Gamma^2})
+       \simeq0.4999968750.
+\]
+
+For the encoded mapping, the certificate gives `g=1.9198`, `b=0.02 sqrt(8)`,
+and success **at most 0.016476688757570787**. Hence the native mapping is
+strictly better for this repair protocol, without needing to simulate the
+encoded evolution. A rational-only separation proof is also supplied, so this
+strict comparison does not rest on unverified floating transcendental output.
+
+Changing only the initial logical state to the optimal `01` reverses the
+preference: encoded retention is **at least 0.9835233112424292**, while native
+retention is approximately **0.5000031250**. This explicitly rules out an
+initial-state-independent preference based only on physical size or chain
+length in this model. Actual representative-readout simulation on the saved
+Zephyr-path programs gives encoded repair about `0.0012909781` and retention
+about `0.9987092787`; the theorem includes those recovered outcomes. The
+separate abstract-path validation also reports strict consistent-state success,
+which is a different measurement event.
+
+The protocol starts at the specified classical encoded state **at the beginning
+of the pause**. It excludes ramp/preparation times and makes no assertion that a
+forward anneal prepares that state. Interpreting the hold as part of reverse
+annealing requires separate ramp analysis. No larger-gap-implies-success
+argument, thermal model, or classical simulated annealing surrogate is used.
+
+## 4. Complexity, reuse, and finite target limits
+
+Let `k=nnz(H)`, `L=n+2 sum(d_r-2)_+`, `E=O(k)`, target size `V_T,E_T`, and
+selected unpruned physical size `Q<=2gL`. Arithmetic-operation costs are:
+
+| Stage | Time | Stored/output size |
+|---|---:|---:|
+| Sparse canonicalization and symbolic QUBO | `O(n+m+k log k)` in this sorted Python implementation | `O(n+m+k)` |
+| Explicit ideal-Zephyr target/template preprocessing | `O(g^2)=O(V_T+E_T)` | `O(g^2)` |
+| Pruned template query | `O(L log L + Q + E)` | `O(Q+E)` |
+| Independent embedding check | `O(V_T+E_T+L+E)` | linear in input/witness |
+| Physical allocation, group scaling, exact rounding certificate | `O(E_T+Q+E)` | `O(E_T+Q+E)` |
+| Tree pause certificate | `O(Q+E)` arithmetic operations | linear input memory |
+| Syndrome/weight numerical QUBO update | linear sparse traversal/output, plus canonical exact-output sorting | `O(n+m+k)` |
+
+For arbitrary labels, sorting costs are explicitly included. Rational bit costs
+also depend on input bit lengths; they are not unit-cost real arithmetic. For
+finite binary64 inputs, numerator/denominator sizes start bounded, and the
+compiler's coefficient sizes grow logarithmically with accumulated term counts.
+The exact-only backend also accepts rational weights, for which common-denominator
+bit size must be charged. The exact transcendental enclosure uses a fixed
+128-bit square-root enclosure and degree-24 exponential bound in its nonvacuous
+regime. The dense scientific validation is exponential, up to `O(8^N_p)` time
+and `O(4^N_p)` memory; it is not part of embedding selection.
+
+For a fixed ideal target, `L<=16g+1` is the deterministic sufficient regime.
+Choosing a larger `g=O(L)` gives `O(L^2)` worst-case hardware/preprocessing/output
+overhead. This is a stated cost, not free extra connectivity or a claim that
+sparsity always yields compact hardware. We never increase the target between
+competing mappings in a comparison.
+
+**Reuse.** Keep a fixed penalty envelope greater than every allowed weight L1
+norm. Syndrome changes touch only the final factors, and weight changes touch
+the original-variable linear terms. `update_instance` changes those numbers,
+copies the sparse output, and updates its exact certificate. The structural
+graph, branches, and target template remain reusable. The practical allocation
+currently rescans the target/groups and recomputes fields, chain strengths, and
+scale; this cost is measured and charged. Any successful automatic embedding
+can also be cached across identical structural graphs. The template's advantage
+is a guaranteed quick new query when the graph changes within capacity, not an
+exclusive ability to cache an unchanged graph.
+
+**Matrix/window changes.** The current implementation recompiles changed `H`
+and obtains fresh pruned branches from the existing target template. It does not
+claim stable auxiliary IDs under arbitrary column insertions or a fully local
+dynamic-minor algorithm. A growing-window example adds two mechanisms and a
+check, then verifies the new embedding. The matrix and complete supplied syndrome
+are the available boundary information. If removed past mechanisms have known
+contribution `b`, the new constraint must use `s_window XOR b`; if that
+contribution is unknown it must remain represented or be modeled explicitly.
+No causal decoder or use of unavailable future detector outcomes is asserted.
+
+## 5. Reproducible evidence and unsuccessful approaches
+
+[results/experiment_summary.json](results/experiment_summary.json) records five
+matrix generators (seed 20261007), complete inputs, compilation/update timings,
+25 mappings, physical sizes/scales, and certificate outcomes. All alternatives
+use ideal `g=6,t=4`: **1,248 target qubits and 11,400 edges**. The explicit
+template has capacity **97**. Automatic reference runs use minorminer 0.2.21,
+seeds `11,29,47`, five-second limits and four tries.
+
+| Sparse matrix | `n,m,k` | QUBO variables / structural edges | Full / pruned template qubits | Automatic qubits, three seeds |
+|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
+| Banded three-body checks | 16,14,42 | 44 / 98 | 516 / 126 | 50,52,52 |
+| Irregular hyperchecks | 18,10,44 | 66 / 154 | 780 / 287 | 88,86,90 |
+| High-degree column, redundant row, isolated column | 18,12,44 | 62 / 140 | 732 / 264 | 82,82,82 |
+| Graphlike incidence | 24,12,48 | 74 / 160 | 876 / 364 | 92,94,95 |
+| Single degree-30 hypercheck | 30,1,30 | 86 / 169 | 1020 / 475 | 93,99,101 |
